RoboEvo2: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness–Policy Co-Evolution

Chenzhi Liu    Jiehong Lin    Wei Huang    Xuzhao Huang    Haoyuan Li    Yang Zhang Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong Zhejiang University Southern University of Science and Technology    Junchao Huang    Chenyeyang Cai    Bo Wang    Kazuhiro Kosuge Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen City University of Hong Kong*Equal contribution †Project leader ‡Corresponding author: xjqi@eee.hku.hkProject page: kaiknower.github.io/RoboEvo2  Code: github.com/kaiknower/RoboEvo2    Zhongrui Wang Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong Zhejiang University Southern University of Science and Technology    Xiaojuan Qi
Abstract

Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo2, a framework for recursive harness–policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo2 improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

1 Introduction

Robots should adapt rapidly to unfamiliar environments, acquire new skills through interaction, and execute those skills efficiently with practice. Human learning motivates this progression from deliberate problem solving to fluent execution, while retaining the flexibility to tackle new situations. Current robot systems offer complementary strengths toward this goal. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) [15, 3, 2, 45] and world action models (WAMs) [41, 11, 13] enable efficient visuomotor control, but remain vulnerable to task and scene shifts [46, 30]. Adapting them through imitation learning often requires collecting many additional human demonstrations, making continual skill acquisition costly. Foundation-model agents can draw on broad prior knowledge, reason about unfamiliar situations, and invoke robot-control APIs to discover and refine solutions [21, 10, 44, 43]. However, repeated reasoning, tool use, and repair introduce latency and API costs that limit reliance on agentic execution for routine behavior.

Realizing this progression requires a reciprocal learning loop between an agent’s harness—its executable skills, memory, and orchestration—and its low-level policy. Harness-centered recursive self-improvement methods refine programs and accumulate experience through feedback [9, 20, 32, 35], but keeping the motor policy fixed does not transfer newly acquired skills into the learned controller. Policy-centered methods use foundation models to guide autonomous data collection and improve learned controllers [12, 47, 23], but do not jointly adapt the harness to the controller’s changing abilities. Co-evolution must therefore connect learning efficient policy behaviors from harness discoveries with adapting the harness to the improving policy. This reciprocity is essential because policy improvement changes both the motor skills available to the agent and the failures that still require exploration and repair.

We introduce RoboEvo2, a framework for recursive harness–policy co-evolution that uses current-policy failures to drive both updates (). In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, a coding agent diagnoses failures, discovers verified corrections, and consolidates them into reusable skills, routing strategies, and persistent memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, successful trajectories and matched failure–correction pairs teach the policy to reproduce effective corrections and disfavor failed alternatives. The updated policy then supplies stronger motor skills for subsequent agentic search, while its remaining failures redirect harness refinement. Concurrent studies also investigate harness–policy coupling [7, 4, 36, 34]. RoboEvo2 connects failure-guided, multi-route solution discovery with explicit learning from matched failures and corrections, progressively reducing repeated agentic intervention as acquired skills are internalized into the policy.

First, to discover complementary capabilities, we develop a failure-conditioned, multi-route P2H repair engine. For each policy failure, it searches three solution routes in parallel: Code refines control programs, Code+ICL incorporates demonstration guidance, and Code+Policy composes programs with learned motor skills. Execution feedback drives iterative repair, and the successful candidate with the lowest normalized motion jerk is selected under matched conditions. This design combines complementary control capabilities to generate verified, smooth corrections targeted at current policy weaknesses.

Second, to internalize corrective capabilities, we introduce Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD). CPD pairs failed and corrected continuations from the same starting state and optimizes a margin between their action-prediction losses relative to a frozen reference policy. Asymmetric proximity penalties discourage degradation of corrective behaviors and excessive suppression of failed alternatives. Combined with supervised learning on verified trajectories, CPD teaches both which corrections to reproduce and which failed alternatives to disfavor. Failure-aware sampling and continual-learning regularization support targeted acquisition and capability retention.

Third, to sustain iterative capability reuse, we develop a harness update mechanism coupled with policy reuse across rounds. Compatible repairs update executable skills and routing logic, while persistent memory retains failure contexts, attempted solutions, and validated guidance. The updated policy then drives subsequent rollouts and participates in Code+Policy search, changing both the failures requiring exploration and the motor primitives available for repair. This closes the reciprocal loop: accumulated harness knowledge supports correction discovery, while internalized policy capabilities directly support subsequent search.

Experiments demonstrate recursive adaptation to distribution shifts without additional human demonstrations. Across eight rounds on LIBERO-PRO [46] and five rounds on RoboTwin C2R [5], standalone success improves from 11.0% to 84.1% and 46.0% to 77.5%, respectively, with hybrid success reaching 90.5% and 87.4% alongside reduced agentic API expenditure. On RoboTwin C2R, our method with 7.5K trajectories matches conventional training with 27.5K trajectories. Ablations validate reciprocal co-evolution, complementary solution routes in P2H, and counterfactual preference distillation in H2P. We further demonstrate autonomous task acquisition on MolmoSpaces [16] and cross-embodiment harness transfer. On the Unitree G1-D, a simulation-evolved harness enables the collection of 120 demonstrations, yielding 85.0% standalone success compared with 80.0% using 200 human demonstrations, while fixed-harness hybrid execution reaches 95.0%.

2 Related Work

Continual Robot Learning. A continually learning policy must retain earlier skills and obtain supervision for new ones. For retention, EWC regularizes weights [17], ER replays data [29], and PackNet isolates parameters [27]. In manipulation, LOTUS builds skill libraries [33] and TAIL uses task-specific adapters [25]. On pretrained VLAs, experience replay mitigates forgetting [24, 48]; PHASER refines it by prioritizing phases most at risk of forgetting [6], while CRL-VLA limits advantage magnitudes on prior tasks during continual RL [42]. For new supervision, HG-DAgger and RECAP draw on human interventions during policy rollouts [14, 1], APO and FlowPRO turn such interventions into preference signals [39, 38], and SOAR uses autonomous VLM-guided practice [47]. RoboEvo2 learns from verified harness repairs of policy failures rather than operator corrections, and employs failure-aware task sampling to retain skills and improve low-success tasks.

Agentic Self-Improvement. Agentic systems such as Code as Policies [21], Harness VLA [44], RATs [43], and ASPIRE [26] solve tasks through programs, skills, and memory without model fine-tuning. Among recursive self-improvement (RSI) frameworks, Zetta, EmbodiedEvo, EmbodiedRSI, and RPG evolve only the harness [9, 20, 32, 35], whereas ENPIRE and EmbodiRSI focus on policy improvement [40, 18]. Co-Harness and Self-HPO alternate harness and model updates for LLM agents [7, 37]. AdaRSI [34] refines its harness and fine-tunes only sub-steps that still fail when retried from saved states. However, these methods train the policy only to imitate successful executions. In contrast, RoboEvo2 also learns from failures: it pairs a failed continuation with a verified repair from the same state and trains the policy to prefer the repair. Repairs are sought in parallel along code-only, demonstration-guided, and policy-calling routes.

3 RoboEvo2

3.1 Overview of Recursive Co-Evolution

RoboEvo2 is a policy-driven framework for recursive harness–policy co-evolution. The current policy exposes capability gaps through execution failures, the harness discovers effective solutions, and the policy subsequently internalizes these corrections. As illustrated in Fig. 2, RoboEvo2 jointly evolves an agentic harness Hr=(Lr,Mr,ρr)H_{r}=(L_{r},M_{r},\rho_{r}) and a neural policy πθr\pi_{\theta_{r}} at evolution round rr.

The harness consists of an executable skill library LrL_{r}, persistent experience memory MrM_{r}, and a routing mechanism ρr\rho_{r} for skill invocation and code–policy coordination. We initialize H0H_{0} with robot APIs and parameterized code-based skills from CaP-X [10] and RATs [43]. The initial policy πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} is obtained by fine-tuning a pretrained VLA or WAM on robot demonstrations 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}.

Each evolution round rr consists of four stages:

(1) Policy Rollouts. The current policy πθr\pi_{\theta_{r}} serves as the primary executor, generating task rollouts 𝒯r\mathcal{T}_{r}. Task-level verification partitions them into successful trajectories 𝒮r\mathcal{S}_{r} and failed trajectories ℱr\mathcal{F}_{r}. The failures identify where additional capabilities are needed.

(2) Policy-to-Harness Evolution (P2H). For each failed rollout, a VLM-based coding agent (GPT-6 Astra) diagnoses the failure and searches for solutions through three complementary routes: Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy. Verified solutions are selected based on execution quality, and compatible improvements are integrated across failures into a candidate harness H~r+1\widetilde{H}_{r+1}. Execution and repair experiences are retained for subsequent reuse (Sec. 3.2).

(3) Harness-to-Policy Evolution (H2P). Successful policy rollouts and harness-generated corrections are accumulated as training data. Matched successful and failed executions further provide counterfactual supervision. Task-balanced, failure-aware sampling and policy optimization produce an updated candidate policy πθ~r+1\pi_{\widetilde{\theta}_{r+1}} (Sec. 3.3).

(4) Evaluation and Selection. We evaluate two execution modes: standalone, where the policy executes tasks independently, and hybrid, where the harness coordinates policy execution with reusable code skills. Candidate and previous versions are compared on matched development tasks, initial states, and execution budgets. Updates are retained when they improve the corresponding success rates; otherwise, previous versions are preserved. The selected pair (Hr+1,πθr+1)(H_{r+1},\pi_{\theta_{r+1}}) enters the next round. Further details are provided in Appendix D.

By repeatedly discovering and internalizing missing capabilities, RoboEvo2 forms a recursive improvement loop driven by the evolving policy’s remaining failures.

3.2 Policy-to-Harness (P2H) Evolution

P2H evolution discovers executable solutions to capability gaps exposed by the current policy. Rather than relying on the coding agent to solve tasks independently from scratch, P2H targets failed policy executions and converts successful corrections into reusable harness capabilities. Given ℱr\mathcal{F}_{r}, it first searches for solutions to individual failures and then consolidates the verified results across tasks.

Failure-Guided Solution Search and Selection. For each failed rollout f∈ℱrf\in\mathcal{F}_{r}, a VLM-based coding agent diagnoses the failure using policy observations, action history, and task outcomes. It retrieves relevant skills from LrL_{r} and past experiences from MrM_{r}, then explores three complementary solution routes in parallel:

  • •

    Code: The agent first attempts recovery using the code-based skills in the current harness. If unsuccessful, it refines executable skills, including motion targets, grasp and contact strategies, phase transitions, and recovery logic based on execution feedback.

  • •

    Code+ICL: The agent randomly samples one demonstration for the target task from 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} to guide harness refinement. It extracts task structure, manipulation strategies, and temporal cues to revise executable skills, including object-relative motions, arm coordination, gripper control, and execution sequencing. The revisions are then tested and iteratively improved via execution feedback.

  • •

    Code+Policy: The agent first attempts recovery by coordinating code-based skills in the current harness with the policy πθr\pi_{\theta_{r}} as a learned motor primitive. If unsuccessful, it refines harness orchestration, including subgoal allocation, skill composition, policy invocation, handoff conditions, and recovery strategies. This route exploits the complementary capabilities of code and learned policies.

The three routes explore different solution strategies while sharing the same task goal and execution constraints. Each route operates in an isolated execution branch, starting from the relevant failure state when feasible or from a matched task reset otherwise. Execution and refinement continue until task success or budget exhaustion, while the policy parameters remain frozen throughout P2H.

Each route retains at most one verified successful program–trajectory pair for failure ff, forming a candidate set 𝒞f+\mathcal{C}_{f}^{+} of up to three solutions. Among successful candidates evaluated under matched conditions, we select the one with the lowest normalized motion jerk J⁡(τ)J(\tau) [19]:

Cf∗=(cf∗,τf∗)∈arg​min(c,τ)∈𝒞f+⁡J​(τ),C_{f}^{*}=(c_{f}^{*},\tau_{f}^{*})\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{(c,\tau)\in\mathcal{C}_{f}^{+}}J(\tau), (1)

where cf∗c_{f}^{*} and τf∗\tau_{f}^{*} denote the selected executable program and verified trajectory, respectively. If no candidate succeeds, the failure remains unresolved and is retained for diagnosis.

Importantly, each resolved failure associates the original failed policy execution with a verified successful correction. These execution records provide targeted supervision for subsequent policy learning, including matched corrective pairs for CPD when the corresponding state and execution conditions are satisfied (Sec. 3.3). Further implementation details are provided in Appendices A and C.

Cross-Failure Harness Integration. Beyond individual recovery, P2H consolidates successful solutions into persistent capabilities that can be reused across tasks. The coding agent merges compatible modifications from selected solutions into a unified candidate harness H~r+1\widetilde{H}_{r+1}.

The skill library LrL_{r} is extended with new or refined executable programs, while the routing mechanism ρr\rho_{r} is updated when skill selection, subgoal coordination, or code–policy switching changes. Meanwhile, memory MrM_{r} accumulates failure contexts, attempted solutions, execution outcomes, and validated repair guidance. Successful recovery does not necessarily require modifying code; solutions using existing skills still contribute verified trajectories and reusable experience. The integrated harness is checked for compatibility and evaluated before replacing HrH_{r}, preventing individual repairs from automatically becoming persistent system updates. Further details are provided in Appendix A.

3.3 Harness-to-Policy (H2P) Evolution

H2P evolution aims to internalize agent-discovered corrective behaviors into the neural policy. It leverages two complementary forms of supervision. First, successful policy rollouts 𝒮r\mathcal{S}_{r} and verified harness-generated trajectories 𝒯rH,+\mathcal{T}_{r}^{H,+}, including full-task solutions and recovery continuations, are accumulated in 𝒟r+1\mathcal{D}_{r+1} for supervised learning. Second, matched policy failures and successful corrections form a corrective preference dataset 𝒫r+1\mathcal{P}_{r+1} for Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD), which encourages the policy to favor corrected behaviors over failed alternatives.

Counterfactual Preference Distillation. We build 𝒫r+1\mathcal{P}_{r+1} by pairing original policy failures with verified harness-generated corrections. For each resolved failure, successful and failed continuations are compared from the same starting state under matched execution conditions. Each valid pair is represented as (x,y+,y−)(x,y^{+},y^{-}), where x=(o,g)x=(o,g) denotes the shared observation and task goal, and y+y^{+} and y−y^{-} denote successful and failed action targets, respectively. Only outcome-verified, state-matched pairs enter 𝒫r+1\mathcal{P}_{r+1}; unmatched successful recoveries remain available in 𝒟r+1\mathcal{D}_{r+1}.

To learn from these corrective pairs, CPD optimizes the relative losses of successful and failed targets against a frozen reference policy. Let ℓθ​(y∣x)\ell_{\theta}(y\mid x) denote the per-sample training loss, and let θ¯r=θr\bar{\theta}_{r}=\theta_{r} denote the frozen policy parameters at the beginning of round rr. We define

δ±=ℓθ​(y±∣x)−ℓθ¯r​(y±∣x),\delta^{\pm}=\ell_{\theta}(y^{\pm}\mid x)-\ell_{\bar{\theta}_{r}}(y^{\pm}\mid x), (2)

with Δ=δ+−δ−\Delta=\delta^{+}-\delta^{-} measuring the change in the successful-versus-failed loss gap relative to the reference policy.

CPD combines a margin-based preference objective with asymmetric proximity constraints:

ℒgap\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}} =𝔼⁡[(max⁡{Δ,−m}+m)2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(\max\{\Delta,-m\}+m\bigr)^{2}\right], (3)
ℒprox\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prox}} =𝔼⁡[[δ+]+2+[δ−−κ]+2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[[\delta^{+}]_{+}^{2}+[\delta^{-}-\kappa]_{+}^{2}\right],

where [z]+=max⁡(z,0)[z]_{+}=\max(z,0), mm is the preference margin, and κ\kappa controls the allowed increase in negative-target loss. The gap term favors successful corrections over failed alternatives, while the asymmetric proximity term prevents degradation on successful targets and excessive suppression of failed ones. Together, they promote corrective behavior learning while maintaining proximity to θ¯r\bar{\theta}_{r}.

Failure-Aware Continual Policy Optimization. To prioritize current capability gaps while mitigating forgetting, we adopt task-balanced, failure-aware sampling for both successful trajectories 𝒟r+1\mathcal{D}_{r+1} and corrective pairs 𝒫r+1\mathcal{P}_{r+1}. Let 𝒦b\mathcal{K}_{b} denote the tasks represented in data pool b∈{𝒟,𝒫}b\in\{\mathcal{D},\mathcal{P}\}, and s^r,k\hat{s}_{r,k} the current policy’s success rate on task kk. With failure weight wr,k=(1−s^r,k)γw_{r,k}=(1-\hat{s}_{r,k})^{\gamma}, we define

pr,k(b)=12​|𝒦b|+wr,k2​∑j∈𝒦bwr,j,p_{r,k}^{(b)}=\frac{1}{2|\mathcal{K}_{b}|}+\frac{w_{r,k}}{2\sum_{j\in\mathcal{K}_{b}}w_{r,j}}, (4)

where γ>0\gamma>0 controls the emphasis on challenging tasks. We independently sample supervised trajectories and corrective pairs from their respective task distributions, balancing historical coverage with targeted improvement. Each policy uses its native supervised objective ℒsup\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}. With compatible corrective pairs, the update objective is

ℒupdate=ℒsup+λpref​(ℒgap+λprox​ℒprox).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{update}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sup}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{pref}}(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{prox}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prox}}). (5)

Without compatible pairs, we set λpref=0\lambda_{\mathrm{pref}}=0. To further mitigate forgetting, we incorporate Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) [17], which penalizes changes to parameters important for previously learned tasks:

ℒtotal=ℒupdate+λEWC2​∑iFr,i​(θi−θ¯r,i)2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{update}}+\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{EWC}}}{2}\sum_{i}F_{r,i}(\theta_{i}-\bar{\theta}_{r,i})^{2}. (6)

Here, ii indexes the policy parameters, λEWC\lambda_{\mathrm{EWC}} controls the regularization strength, and Fr,iF_{r,i} estimates the importance of parameter ii using squared per-example gradients.

After offline co-evolution, compatible action policies can be further refined using PPO [31], which collects fresh simulator rollouts and optimizes task-success rewards.

3.4 Standalone and Hybrid Execution Modes

RoboEvo2 supports two complementary execution modes that balance policy autonomy and agentic assistance:

  • •

    Standalone Execution: The co-evolved policy executes tasks directly without coding-agent intervention, enabling efficient neural inference while leveraging capabilities acquired from agentic corrections.

  • •

    Hybrid Execution: An embodied agent coordinates the co-evolved policy with reusable code skills, supporting explicit task decomposition, skill composition, and feedback-driven recovery [44].

Through recursive co-evolution, policy failures drive the discovery of new executable capabilities, while agentic corrections are progressively internalized into the policy. As the policy improves, its evolving capability gaps guide subsequent harness evolution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle of discovery and learning. This process aims to amortize costly agentic reasoning into efficient policy execution, progressively reducing reliance on agentic assistance while retaining the harness for unresolved challenges.

4 Experiments

We evaluate RoboEvo2 on LIBERO-PRO [46] and RoboTwin C2R [5] for multi-round co-evolution and generalization to unseen perturbations, with ablations examining reciprocal evolution, P2H solution routes, and CPD. MolmoSpaces [16] evaluates autonomous capability acquisition, while cross-embodiment and Unitree G1-D experiments demonstrate harness reusability, sim-to-real transfer, and real-world policy learning.

4.1 Generalization and Multi-Round Evolution

We evaluate RoboEvo2 on two benchmarks under distribution shifts. LIBERO-PRO [46] transfers policies trained on original LIBERO demonstrations to task and position perturbations, while RoboTwin C2R [5] adapts policies trained on 2,500 clean demonstrations to randomized scenes across 50 bimanual tasks. On both benchmarks, evolution runs on seeds held out from the initial training data without additional human annotation, and generalization is evaluated on separate unseen seeds (800 LIBERO-PRO and 5,000 RoboTwin C2R episodes; Appendix D).

Multi-Round Adaptation and Data Efficiency. Figure 3 demonstrates progressive improvements in standalone and hybrid execution. On LIBERO-PRO, eight rounds improve standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5%, while API expenditure decreases from $430.63 to $98.92. On RoboTwin C2R, five rounds increase standalone success from 46.0% to 77.5% and hybrid success from 48.8% to 87.4%, with API expenditure decreasing from $719.05 to $323.84. These results demonstrate sustained capability improvement alongside decreasing agentic costs, highlighting the benefits of recursive harness–policy co-evolution.

Beyond execution efficiency, RoboEvo2 acquires training experience without additional human demonstrations. As shown in Tab. 1, starting from 2,500 clean demonstrations, our framework autonomously collects 5,000 verified trajectories and achieves 77.5% standalone success on RoboTwin C2R. With the same 7.5K trajectories, clean+random training reaches only 67.2%, and it needs 27.5K to reach 76.8%. RoboEvo2 thus matches it with only 27.3% of the training data, suggesting that failure-driven experience provides effective supervision.

Comparison with Self-Evolving Methods. Table 2 compares RoboEvo2 with recent self-evolving robot systems. Harness-centered methods, including ASPIRE [26], Zetta [9], DynaHarness [8], and EmbodiedRSI [32], primarily improve executable skills and agentic recovery. In contrast, RoboEvo2 enables reciprocal evolution, where harness discoveries provide corrective supervision for policy learning, while the updated policy supplies stronger motor primitives and guides subsequent harness search. Across all eight LIBERO-PRO settings, RoboEvo2 achieves 84.1% standalone and 90.5% hybrid success, surpassing EmbodiedRSI’s 86.8% hybrid success. Further PPO refinement increases standalone and hybrid success to 94.8% and 96.8%, respectively. These results demonstrate competitive adaptation performance while progressively internalizing agent-discovered capabilities into the policy.

4.2 Ablation Studies

We conduct ablation studies on LIBERO-PRO to evaluate the contributions of individual components in RoboEvo2.

Effect of Joint Harness–Policy Evolution. We compare full RoboEvo2 with two variants that freeze either the policy (P2H only) or the harness (H2P only). As shown in Tab. 3, full co-evolution consistently outperforms both variants, reaching 52.3% standalone and 68.3% hybrid success after three rounds. Notably, its standalone advantage over H2P only increases across rounds, suggesting that evolving harness capabilities provide increasingly effective supervision for policy learning. These results highlight the benefits of reciprocal capability discovery and internalization over one-sided evolution.

Effect of Complementary P2H Solution Routes. Starting from the same policy rollouts with an initial standalone success rate of 11.0%, we evaluate Code, Code+ICL, Code+Policy, and their combination in the first evolution round. Each route first attempts execution using the existing harness without modification, then iteratively repairs failed executions through feedback-driven refinement. As shown in Tab. 4, all routes recover additional failures, with Code+Policy achieving the largest individual gain of 14.8 points. Combining all routes achieves the highest success rate of 49.1%, highlighting their complementary problem-solving capabilities. Training on the collected trajectories further improves standalone policy success from 11.0% to 32.1% with all routes, showing that complementary discovery supports policy internalization.

Effect of CPD Loss Components. Through P2H evolution, multi-route agentic recovery produces successful corrections to policy failures, providing matched corrective pairs for H2P learning. We evaluate the preference gap ℒgap\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gap}} and asymmetric proximity term ℒprox\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prox}} using these pairs under identical training data, initialization, and EWC settings. As shown in Tab. 5, adding the preference gap to supervised learning improves standalone success from 20.1% to 29.9%. The full CPD objective further increases success to 32.1%, demonstrating the benefit of asymmetric proximity constraints for corrective capability internalization.

4.3 Capability Acquisition and Transfer

We further investigate whether RoboEvo2 can autonomously acquire manipulation capabilities and reuse evolved skills across robot embodiments.

Autonomous Task Acquisition. MolmoSpaces [16] evaluates autonomous manipulation skill acquisition, where agents propose scene-grounded goals and discover executable solutions through exploration. Unlike code-only agents such as CaP-Agent0 [10] and RATs [43], we extend the exploration process of RATs by incorporating a trainable policy within our harness–policy co-evolution framework. Verified agentic executions are used to improve the policy, enabling acquired skills to be internalized beyond executable programs. Across 40 tasks spanning opening, closing, picking, and pick-and-place, our standalone policy achieves 57.0% success, compared with 38.0% for RATs, while hybrid execution further reaches 65.8% (Tab. 6).

Cross-Embodiment Harness Transfer. We evaluate whether the harness evolved on RoboTwin with ALOHA AgileX can be directly reused across robot embodiments. Keeping the same 50 tasks, 20 held-out layouts per task, executable skills, routing logic, and persistent memory, we replace the robot with dual ARX-X5 or dual Franka-Panda, adapting only the robot-specific control interfaces. As shown in Tab. 7, the frozen harness achieves 45.8% success on ALOHA AgileX, 42.5% on dual ARX-X5, and 41.0% on dual Franka-Panda. The small performance drops indicate that evolved harness capabilities can transfer across robot embodiments without additional skill evolution.

4.4 Real-World Robot Manipulation

We evaluate RoboEvo2 on four bimanual tasks (Fig. 4) using the Unitree G1-D, investigating whether simulation-evolved harness capabilities can transfer to physical robots and provide training supervision without teleoperation.

Harness Transfer and Autonomous Data Collection. We directly transfer the harness evolved on RoboTwin to the Unitree G1-D, adapting only the robot interfaces and estimating motion targets from real observations. Using its frozen Code route, the transferred harness collects 10 verified demonstrations per task. We first fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5} on these trajectories and execute the resulting policy on the physical robot. When execution fails, an operator approximately restores the robot and scene to the pre-failure state, without teleoperating the corrective actions. The agent then explores Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, selecting verified corrections with the lowest normalized motion jerk. This process collects 20 additional successful trajectories per task, yielding 120 automatically generated demonstrations in total. We use these trajectories and eligible corrective pairs to train the final standalone policy through H2P.

Real-World Results. As shown in Tab. 8, the transferred harness achieves 47.5% mean success without target-side skill evolution. The RoboEvo2 policy trained on 120 automatically collected demonstrations achieves 85.0% standalone success, compared with 80.0% for a π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline trained on 200 human-teleoperated demonstrations. Combining the learned policy with the fixed harness further increases success to 95.0%. These results demonstrate that reusable harness capabilities can support sim-to-real execution and generate effective policy supervision with limited human intervention, while hybrid execution continues to complement the learned policy.

5 Conclusion

We presented RoboEvo2, a framework for failure-driven recursive harness–policy co-evolution. Through complementary solution discovery (P2H) and counterfactual capability internalization (H2P), verified agentic corrections become reusable harness skills and learned policy behaviors. Across rounds, the improved policy provides stronger motor primitives and redirects subsequent harness exploration, closing the reciprocal learning loop. Experiments demonstrate progressive improvements in standalone and hybrid execution with reduced agentic costs, alongside data-efficient adaptation, autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment reuse, and real-world policy learning. RoboEvo2 thus supports progressive policy autonomy while retaining agentic capabilities for unresolved challenges.

LLM Usage Statement

An LLM-based assistant (OpenAI Codex) was used for language editing, LaTeX formatting, and checking bibliographic metadata. All assisted content was reviewed and verified by the authors. Separately, as part of the method, RoboEvo2 uses GPT-6 Astra as its coding agent (Qwen3.8-27B in the agent-backbone ablation; see Appendix G). No LLM is listed as an author; the authors take full responsibility for the manuscript, implementation, experiments, and scientific claims.

Appendix A Harness Details

A.1 Agent, Skill Library, Memory, and Routing

Coding agent.

The agent is GPT-6 Astra (gpt-6-astra), run with reasoning effort xhigh; it is used both for coding and for demonstration video analysis. Each coding call receives the task instruction, recorded camera frames, the localized failure, retrieved memory entries, and the editable skill programs, and returns a program revision; the prompts are given in Appendix E. After each round we save the accepted code, memory, policy checkpoint, and data manifest.

Skill library.

The skill library LrL_{r} holds only executable code, separate from memory MrM_{r} and routing ρr\rho_{r}. It is organized as a two-level skill tree. At the bottom are atomic skills: observing, gripper commands, relative motions, motions to a target anchored at an image pixel, and policy calls, which only Code+Policy may use. Above them are composite skills, each composed from atomic skills and parameterized by its arguments, such as grasping, placing, transferring, pulling, and stroking along a surface. A program calls skills by name with arguments. Extending LrL_{r} adds a new entry, and refining a skill writes a new revision of its entry while earlier revisions are kept. Figure 6 shows how general skills are specialized and how memory grows on LIBERO-PRO.

Memory.

Memory MrM_{r} has two parts. General memory holds lessons that apply across tasks, grouped by skill category (perception, grasping, placing, contact, policy, and motion and planning). Experiences are learned from individual tasks: each entry states when it applies, the action to take, and the skills it uses, and is retrieved by matching the task instruction. An experience that holds across tasks is promoted to general memory (Fig. 6).

Routing.

Routing ρr\rho_{r} is a set of rules in the agent’s instructions rather than a separate model. In hybrid execution, code staging precedes each policy call, and after the call the agent re-observes before choosing the next step. Updating ρr\rho_{r} edits these rules. Figure 5 shows the routing on one recorded LIBERO-PRO episode.

A.2 Solution Routes

Route capabilities.

Each route evolves its own skill library and memory from the same initial harness; the routes use the same coding model, observations, verifier, and budgets and differ only in what else the agent may use. Code calls code skills only and receives no demonstration. Code+ICL additionally receives a demonstration of the task in context and cannot call the policy. Code+Policy can additionally call the current policy with a short local instruction, and receives no demonstration. In every route, the agent’s program is executed from the failure state or from the original reset; the failure state is restored by replaying the policy’s recorded actions. Each repair work item contains the parent harness revision, the task and its initial state, the original goal and verifier, the localized failure, the affected skill, retrieved repair cases, and a trial budget. Figure 7 shows the three routes on one LIBERO-PRO case, turn off the stove.

In-context demonstrations.

On LIBERO-PRO, the Code+ICL demonstration of a task is an episode of a similar task from the official LIBERO training demonstrations, chosen without regard to outcome or quality. Frames similar to the current views are selected from both cameras and given with the recorded robot state and action at each frame. The agent is told that the demonstration shows a different scene and grounds every target in the current views.

Appendix B Repair Examples

A validated repair is written back as a revision of a general skill in LrL_{r} or, for policy orchestration, of the routing rules ρr\rho_{r} (Sec. A.1).

Figure 8 lists when each repair applies, what it changes, and what it edits; the revision is kept only if the complete task succeeds and earlier successes that use the edited skill still succeed.

Appendix C Policy Training Details

C.1 Training Setup and Data

Tables 9, 10, 11 and 12 list the policy training setup on each benchmark and on the G1-D robot. Training data come from successful policy rollouts and from verified harness-generated trajectories of two kinds: full-task solutions from a matched task reset, and recovery continuations from the state where the policy failed, within the remaining horizon. In each group of executions that share a start state and source type, the smoothest success is kept (Sec. C.2). Records store the source state, instruction, policy and harness versions, actions, remaining horizon, outcome, and cost.

Appendix D Evaluation Protocol

Standalone success runs the policy alone, without the harness or any agent call; hybrid success runs the same policy with the harness, which routes each step to the policy or a code skill. Table 13 lists the evaluation tasks. Table 14 compares the information available to the agent in Harness VLA [44] and in RoboEvo2. Table 15 lists the real-robot configuration.

Appendix E Agent Prompts

The agent uses two prompts: the execution prompt writes and revises programs from the current views, and the evolution prompt modifies the harness itself (skills, memory, and routing rules) from recorded failures.

⬇
You control a robot from the current camera images and the robot state.
## OBSERVATION
The instruction is the task; no object poses, simulator state, or rewards are available. Select targets as pixels in the current views and never invent world coordinates.
## SKILLS
Call only the listed skills, within their step and motion limits.
## ROUTE
<route>
## RESPONSE FORMAT
Before finishing, check every requested object and relation in the current views. Return one JSON object with a brief visual hypothesis, the skill calls, and the next step:
{"hypothesis": "<visual hypothesis>",
"operations": [<skill calls>],
"next": "reobserve" | "finish"}

The ROUTE section of each route reads:

⬇
Code: Only code skills are available; no demonstration is attached and the policy cannot be called.
Code+ICL: The policy cannot be called. The demonstration shows a different scene; transfer its strategy, not its object locations.
Code+Policy: For local contact you may call the policy with one short instruction and a step budget, e.g.
{"op": "vla_act", "prompt": "grasp the visible white mug", "steps": 40}
Stage with code skills first and re-observe after the call.

The user message is one JSON object followed by the current RGB and depth images of each camera view; the demonstration field is present only on Code+ICL:

⬇
{"instruction": "<instruction>",
"cameras": {"<view>": <image size, intrinsics,
camera-to-world>},
"robot": <robot state>,
"remaining_steps": <steps>,
"remaining_revisions": <programs>,
"skills": <skill catalog>,
"general_lessons": <retrieved lessons>,
"reusable_experiences":
<retrieved experiences>,
"previous_public_execution": <status of each
call, executed actions, end-effector error,
stop reason>,
"training_demonstration":
<demonstration frames>}
<view> current RGB: <image>
<view> current depth: <image>

The evolution system prompt is:

⬇
You improve the harness from its own failures.
## DIAGNOSIS
Diagnose each failure from the recorded frames.
## CHANGES
Revise the affected skill or add a new one. Record what you learned as memory entries that cite the attempts supporting them. Edit the routing rules when a phase should move between the policy and code skills. Work on a private copy and test each change within the trial budget.
## ACCEPTANCE
A change is kept only if the complete task then succeeds and earlier successes that use the edited skills still succeed.
## RESPONSE FORMAT
Return a patch, a memory delta with its evidence, and the attempted trajectories.

and its user message is:

⬇

Harness: <skill code, memory, routing rules>
Similar repairs: <retrieved cases>

Appendix H Limitations

RoboEvo2 composes and revises skills on top of a fixed set of atomic skills and perception tools, which do not yet cover capabilities such as force-controlled contact or in-hand regrasping. Future work can enlarge this initial library with such primitives, which the agent can then compose and revise like the existing ones. A task-level success check selects the executions that train the policy; the VLM check that repaired skills already use could replace it, at the cost of extra model calls.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.

We gratefully acknowledge support from our major funders, member institutions, , and all contributors.
